newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish minister sees fast progress on Vatican pact.
newsitem.headline: Polish minister sees fast progress on Vatican pact.

text.p: Foreign Minister Dariusz Rosati said on Tuesday he hoped Poland was about to clinch a long-delayed Concordat with the Vatican, which has for years been at the centre of domestic political rows.

Rosati, just returned from talks at the Vatican in which both sides agreed a compromise over disputed aspects of the proposed treaty, was asked if he thought it could be accepted by Poland's government and parliament before Pope John Paul ll starts an 11-day visit to his native land on May 31.
"You are asking about my (personal) view. I think this is very likely," Rosati told reporters at a news conference.

But the secular-minded ruling ex-communist party which dominates Poland's parliament made clear it was in no hurry to back ratification of the treaty, which would govern relations between the Polish state and the powerful church.
The Democratic Left Alliance (SLD) and other leftists voted down a motion proposing faster action on ratification.
SLD deputy Izabella Sierakowska told Polish Radio she still had grave doubts about the concordat and questioned whether the declaration agreed by Rosati in Rome would settle them.
The Concordat was signed by in 1993 by a previous, pro-church centre-right government just before it lost parliamentary polls to the ex-communists and a peasant party.
The ex-communists refused to ratify the treaty, arguing that it would surrender too much influence to the Holy See.

The years of delay since then have been held up by the rightist opposition as proof of continued hostility to Catholicism by the former communists and have been an issue in early campaigning for parliamentary polls due around September.
President Aleksander Kwasniewski and Rosati, who are both linked to the SLD but not current members, have argued for the ratification if only to show that Poland honours treaties.

Kwasniewski and Rosati met the Pope at the Vatican on Monday and the foreign minister held talks with top Church officials who approved the declaration settling contentious points of the concordat -- such as whether the state should pay for religious education.

Critics of the concordat have long argued that it should only be adopted after parliamment approves a new Polish constitution, replacing the communist-era document of 1952, which would lay down ground-rules of church-state ties.
Parliament has now approved a draft constitution, fiercely criticised by Catholic, rightist opposition parties including the Solidarity trade union.
This constitution is to be put to a popular referendum on May 25, shortly before the Papal visit.
Acceptance by parliament of the concordat before the elections in September might take some wind out of the sails of the right who accuse the ex-communists of militant anti-clericalism.

If the ex-communists appear to resist ratification to the last they also stand to keep the sympathy of their electorate including many Poles who resent church pressure over such issues as abortion, recently liberalised despite Catholic protests.
